title: Hoax bomb threats hit dozens of flights across Europe in a week
seoTitle: Europe flight bomb threats: what we know
dek: Flights have been diverted and escorted by fighter jets since 2 November, with no explosives reported found. The EU says it is too early to say whether the threats are linked.
happened: On 2 November a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Sofia was diverted to Budapest after a bomb threat. More threats followed on 3 November and again on 5 November, when Ryanair, Finnair, Wizz Air, Aegean and Aer Lingus flights were among those targeted and four planes bound for Prague were searched. Aer Lingus flight EI402 from Dublin to Rome, with 151 passengers and six crew, was escorted by French fighter jets to the Évreux air base. On 6 November The National counted at least 25 more alerts; a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome landed in Venice, and France reported four new threats. That morning the Dublin offices of RTÉ and the Irish Independent were evacuated after emailed threats, and Newstalk said the calls were a hoax. No explosives have been reported found on any flight.

sides.says: EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas said "Any threats against civilians are unacceptable" and that it was "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked". UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called them "malicious hoax threats". Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said: "It is worrying, and we take the threat seriously." Czech police said they "perceive the credibility of the threats as low".
Finnair said two flights "faced unfounded hoax bomb scares" and landed safely, and Aegean called the threats against its flights "baseless".

sides.who: French authorities on the Aer Lingus flight
sides.says: Évreux prosecutor Rémi Coutin said the pilot "allegedly refused" to land at the military base, "preferring a civilian airport". The Prime Minister's office said the jets were ordered up because the pilot "did not cooperate as expected". The prosecutor's office opened an investigation, and the pilot and co-pilot were questioned, then allowed to leave.

sides.who: Aer Lingus and the pilots' union
sides.says: The airline said the crew "acted impeccably and were thoroughly professional". The Irish Air Line Pilots' Association said both pilots "cooperated fully with the French authorities" and called the questioning "generally standard procedure".

sides.who: What is known about the source
sides.says: No one has been publicly identified. An email to Rome's Fiumicino airport was signed on behalf of a self-described anti-feminist group, according to AP and The Journal; AP said it was unclear whether another airport's similar threat came from the same group. Bogotá City Hall said a threat was sent from an account tied to one of its public health networks, and that international hackers may have used the accounts. Euronews says motives are unknown, and notes that authorities sometimes link hybrid attacks in Europe to Russia or Iran; no authority has made that link for these threats in the reports read here.

next: French authorities say an investigation is under way into the source of the alerts, and authorities are investigating the threat to a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon on 6 November. Copenhagen Airport re-screened baggage after police received hostile intelligence about air traffic. The EU says it is following events with national authorities.
summary: Since 2 November anonymous emails and phone calls have warned of bombs on passenger flights across Europe, leading to diversions, searches and fighter escorts, particularly on low-cost carriers and on routes to or from Bulgaria, the Czech Republic and Italy. All the planes landed safely and no explosives have been reported found. France opened an inquiry after an Aer Lingus pilot allegedly declined to land at a military base; the airline and the pilots' union say the crew behaved properly. No one has been publicly identified as responsible, and the EU says it is too early to say whether the threats are linked.

conflicts: Newsrooms count the threats differently. For 3 November, The National says at least seven flights and a cruise ship, The Journal ten planes, and Euronews at least 27. For 5 November, Euronews says at least 25 flights and The National nearly 30 by the end of the day.

On the Aer Lingus flight, the French prosecutor and Prime Minister's office say the pilot did not comply at first; the airline and the pilots' union say the crew behaved properly and cooperated fully.
